Family Health

Hyperthyroidism in men: symptoms, sexual health and treatment

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An overactive thyroid can affect a man’s energy, heartbeat, strength and sexual health. Recognising the full pattern helps guide testing, but neither a sexual symptom nor a semen result can identify the cause by itself.

An overactive thyroid can affect men too

The thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped gland at the front of the neck. Its hormones influence energy use, temperature and the work of organs such as the heart. Hyperthyroidism means that the gland produces too much thyroid hormone; hypothyroidism means that production is too low.

Although hyperthyroidism is more common in women, men can develop it at different ages. It should not be dismissed because it is less common in men. Untreated hormone excess can affect the heart, muscles and bones, and it may contribute to sexual or reproductive problems. Symptoms and blood tests need to be considered together.

Graves’ disease is a common cause

Graves’ disease is an autoimmune condition in which antibodies stimulate the thyroid to make excess hormone. It is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. It can begin in younger or middle-aged adults, but an age range cannot establish or rule out the diagnosis.

The gland may enlarge, and some people develop thyroid eye disease. Eye irritation, swelling, double vision or changes in appearance deserve mention at the appointment. Not everyone with Graves’ disease has obvious neck or eye changes, so their absence does not exclude it.

Nodules, thyroiditis and excess iodine are different causes

One or more thyroid nodules can produce excess hormone independently of the usual control signals. Toxic multinodular goitre is sometimes called Plummer disease. It is more often encountered with increasing age; most thyroid nodules are not cancer, and the word toxic refers to hormone production rather than a poison.

Thyroiditis is inflammation that can release hormone already stored in the gland. This can create a period of hormone excess without sustained overproduction, sometimes followed by low hormone levels. The distinction matters because a medicine that blocks new hormone production may not help that process.

Excess iodine from certain medicines or supplements can also contribute in susceptible people. Include iodine or kelp products, heart medicines such as amiodarone, and any prescribed thyroid replacement in the medication history. Do not stop a necessary medicine yourself; the clinician needs to identify the cause before adjusting treatment.

Symptoms often appear in several parts of life

Possible symptoms include weight loss despite an unchanged or increased appetite, a racing or irregular heartbeat, hand or finger tremor, sweating and difficulty tolerating heat. Frequent bowel movements, trouble sleeping, nervousness, irritability and persistent tiredness may also occur. Feeling overstimulated and exhausted at the same time is possible.

Symptoms may develop gradually and can be mistaken for stress or another illness. Hair thinning and muscle weakness can accompany the other changes. These features are not unique to thyroid disease, and neither cold intolerance nor early baldness alone is a reliable indicator of an overactive thyroid. Keep track of the pattern instead of using one symptom as a diagnosis.

Muscle, bone and breast changes deserve assessment

Ongoing hormone excess can reduce muscle strength and contribute to loss of muscle mass. Osteoporosis can affect men as well as women, so bone health should not be overlooked when thyroid disease is prolonged or other fracture risks are present. The appropriate assessment depends on the individual rather than a scan being necessary for everyone.

Some men develop gynecomastia, an increase in breast glandular tissue related to changes in hormone balance. It has many possible causes, including medicines and conditions unrelated to the thyroid. Report new breast enlargement or a distinct lump rather than assuming thyroid treatment will explain every breast change.

Sexual symptoms are worth discussing directly

Erectile difficulties, a change in desire or problems with ejaculation can occur alongside thyroid dysfunction. Both an overactive and an underactive thyroid may be relevant. It is not accurate to assume that hyperthyroidism always has a stronger relationship with erectile dysfunction, or that every sexual symptom comes from the thyroid.

Diabetes, vascular health, medicines, sleep, emotional strain and relationship circumstances may also need attention. Explain when the difficulty began and whether it changed with other symptoms or treatment. A clinician can assess several contributors at once; there is no need to wait until the thyroid is fully controlled before mentioning a concern.

Testosterone results need careful interpretation

Thyroid hormone excess can raise sex hormone-binding globulin, or SHBG, a protein that carries sex hormones in blood. Total testosterone may rise with it. The free and other available fractions do not necessarily change in the same direction, so saying that hyperthyroidism always lowers testosterone is misleading.

A small study that included nine men with Graves’ disease found higher total testosterone and SHBG during hyperthyroidism without a significant change in mean free testosterone concentration. That does not predict every individual result. Symptoms, timing of sampling and the full laboratory picture guide interpretation rather than one isolated testosterone number.

How thyroid hormones may affect semen

Thyroid hormones act on testicular cells, including testosterone-producing Leydig cells and cells involved in supporting sperm development. A 2018 review discussed animal and human research linking thyroid dysfunction with semen changes. It was a review of existing studies, not a new trial proving that every man with hyperthyroidism becomes infertile.

Reported changes include sperm concentration, motility, shape and sometimes semen volume. Motility means how sperm move; morphology describes their shape. The review also described small study groups, differing assessment methods and uncertainty about mild or subclinical disease. These findings support considering thyroid disease when clinically appropriate, without turning a semen result into a thyroid diagnosis.

Treatment may help, but pregnancy is not guaranteed

In a 2002 controlled study, 23 men with hyperthyroidism were compared with 15 controls and reassessed after thyroid control. Sperm motility was lower before treatment and improved afterwards. Differences in sperm density and morphology were not statistically significant in the same way. This distinction matters when describing what the research actually showed.

The study was small and assessed semen measurements, not a guaranteed pregnancy or live birth for each couple. Improvement in thyroid health may help sexual or reproductive function, but persistent difficulties can have additional causes. Follow-up should assess the concern that matters to the person rather than assume that a normal thyroid blood test completes fertility care.

A fertility assessment looks beyond one hormone

If conception is taking longer than expected, a clinician may review reproductive history, examine the testes and arrange semen analysis. Results sometimes need repeating. When a couple is trying to conceive, assessment may involve both partners rather than assuming that one abnormal result explains everything.

Hormone tests are selected according to symptoms, examination and semen findings. Thyroid testing can be appropriate when thyroid disease is suspected; it is not an automatic requirement after every sperm count. Do not start testosterone or a hormone supplement as a fertility remedy: external testosterone can suppress sperm production.

The assessment begins with your history and examination

Explain your symptoms, family history, past thyroid disease and all medicines or supplements. Older age or a family history can affect clinical suspicion, but neither replaces an assessment. Type 2 diabetes alone is not a reason for routine thyroid testing under NICE guidance; symptoms and other indications still matter.

The clinician may check the thyroid, pulse, tremor, skin, eyes and reflexes. Brisk reflexes or visible changes can provide clues but cannot confirm the diagnosis. Mention sexual, breast or fertility concerns explicitly, even if the appointment initially focuses on palpitations or weight loss.

Blood tests identify the hormone pattern

TSH stands for thyroid-stimulating hormone. In adults without suspected pituitary disease, testing commonly begins with TSH; a low result is followed by free T4 and free T3. Overt hyperthyroidism usually produces low TSH with raised T4 and/or T3. Antibody tests or selected imaging can help identify why it is happening.

High-dose biotin in supplements can distort some thyroid blood tests. Tell the clinician and laboratory what you take and follow their instructions. An ultrasound or uptake scan is chosen for a reason rather than performed in every case. Ask what the results show about both the hormone level and the underlying cause.

Medicines can control production and symptoms

Antithyroid medicines such as methimazole reduce new hormone production. They are different from replacement thyroid hormone, which is used when hormone levels are too low. Treatment takes monitoring and adjustment; improvement is not necessarily immediate, and the course depends on the condition and response.

A beta blocker may be used for symptoms such as a fast pulse or tremor while other treatment works. It does not itself correct excess hormone production. Not every medicine is suitable for every person, and treatment for thyroiditis differs from treatment for Graves’ disease or an overactive nodule.

Know the important medicine warning signs

Antithyroid drugs can rarely cause a dangerous fall in white blood cells. If you develop fever or a severe sore throat while taking one, seek medical care immediately for a blood count and do not take further doses until a clinician clears you to restart.

Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or other possible liver symptoms also requires immediate medical advice. Ask for written instructions when treatment begins, including who to contact outside usual hours. These warnings should sit alongside the routine monitoring plan rather than be left until a problem occurs.

Radioactive iodine and surgery are other options

Radioactive iodine-131 is taken by mouth and acts on thyroid tissue over time. It may be recommended for Graves’ disease or toxic nodules; some people require another treatment. Low thyroid hormone levels can develop afterwards and require replacement. Discuss eye disease, radiation precautions and any plans to father a child with the treating team before treatment.

Surgery removes part or all of the thyroid, depending on the condition. Removal of the whole gland requires lifelong hormone replacement; after partial removal, the need depends on remaining function. Choosing between medicines, radioactive iodine and surgery involves the cause, symptoms, other health conditions, preferences and the risks of each option.

Follow-up matters even when symptoms are mild

A low TSH with normal T4 and T3 is called subclinical hyperthyroidism. Some people are monitored rather than treated immediately, depending on the cause, persistence, age and heart or bone risks. Few symptoms do not mean that an abnormal result should simply be ignored, but they also do not make one treatment mandatory.

Attend agreed blood tests and review appointments, and report continuing sexual or fertility difficulties. Seek emergency care for a very fast heartbeat with high temperature, severe agitation, confusion or collapse, which can signal a rare thyroid storm. Chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness also needs urgent assessment. The aim is a stable thyroid level and a plan for the symptoms that remain.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Thyroid-related sexual and semen changes are possible, but the research does not establish infertility or guaranteed recovery for every man.

SHBG can alter testosterone interpretation. Testing and treatment depend on clinical context; type 2 diabetes alone does not mandate thyroid screening.

How BeMama can help

Bring a symptom timeline and medicine list, including supplements, and mention fertility plans when comparing treatment options.

When to seek help

Endocrinology and reproductive-urology review remain pending. Follow urgent instructions for medicine reactions and severe systemic symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Men can develop hyperthyroidism despite its greater prevalence in women.
  • The cause determines which treatment is appropriate.
  • Total testosterone, free testosterone and SHBG are not interchangeable.
  • Better thyroid control may help sexual or semen changes without guaranteeing pregnancy.

Frequently asked questions

Can men have an overactive thyroid?

Yes. It is less common in men, but symptoms such as unexplained weight loss, tremor or a racing pulse still deserve assessment.

Does Graves’ disease mean the thyroid is being destroyed?

Graves’ antibodies stimulate excess production. That is different from thyroiditis, which can release hormone stored in an inflamed gland.

Does hyperthyroidism always lower testosterone?

No. SHBG and total testosterone may rise, while available fractions can behave differently. A clinician needs to interpret the full pattern.

Does it make every man infertile?

No. Semen changes have been reported, but small studies cannot predict an individual’s ability to conceive.

What did the small treatment study actually show?

Sperm motility improved after thyroid control. Count and shape findings were less clear, and the study did not establish a guaranteed pregnancy outcome.

Should every semen test be followed by a thyroid test?

No. Thyroid testing is chosen according to clinical suspicion and the wider assessment, rather than automatically after every semen analysis.

Does type 2 diabetes alone mean I need thyroid screening?

NICE does not recommend testing solely for type 2 diabetes. Symptoms, examination or other indications can still justify it.

Why should I mention a hair or nail supplement?

Some contain high-dose biotin, which can interfere with thyroid tests. Tell the clinician and laboratory and follow their instructions.

What if I have a fever or severe sore throat on an antithyroid drug?

Seek immediate medical care for a blood count and take no further doses until a clinician says it is safe to restart.

Will surgery always mean lifelong replacement?

Removing the entire thyroid requires lifelong replacement. After partial surgery, the need depends on the remaining gland’s function and follow-up tests.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
